verdicts.claim: Automatic checkpoints run in PASSIVE mode. An automatic checkpoint is triggered by a COMMIT that leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more, or by
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 3.1: 'automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection ... closes'; pragma.html: 'All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE.'

verdicts.claim: There are four checkpoint modes: PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE. PASSIVE copies as many frames as it can without waiting for rea
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: 'busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode ... passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished'. Note c3ref also lists a fifth value, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP, which checkpoints zero frames.

verdicts.claim: FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE block until no writer is active and all readers use the latest snapshot. They also take the exclusive writer
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: 'FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock'; wal.html: 'FULL and RESTART checkpoints ... can only be initiated by a call to sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2()' (the pragma wraps v2).

verdicts.claim: RESTART adds a wait until all readers read from the database file only, so the next writer restarts the WAL from the beginning. TRUN
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.' Tension: c3ref says RESTART 'does not impede readers'.

verdicts.claim: A checkpoint cannot copy past the end mark of any active reader. It stops at the first WAL page that a reader still needs, so a long
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 2.1: 'must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader ... remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got'.

verdicts.claim: After a fully checkpointed WAL and no active readers, the next writer rewinds the WAL to the start and reuses it. A plain checkpoint d
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 6: 'The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.'

verdicts.claim: Automatic checkpointing is enabled by default. It runs a PASSIVE checkpoint when the WAL is N pages or longer, with N = 1000 unless SQ
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Setting the auto-checkpoint size to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off ... enabled by default with an interval of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT.'

verdicts.claim: PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback. FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE invoke it while they wait for the writer lock and for rea
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: 'If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.'

verdicts.claim: By default SQLite runs an automatic checkpoint when the WAL reaches 1000 pages, on the same thread that performs the COMMIT.
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT'; page 'last updated on 2026-08-25'.

verdicts.claim: After a successful TRUNCATE checkpoint, the WAL file is zero bytes and both pnLog and pnCkpt are zero. A TRUNCATE checkpoint that retu
verdicts.evidence: c3ref: 'upon successful completion of an SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE ... both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero'; the SQLITE_BUSY-leaves-size half is implied by 'truncates ... just prior to a successful return', not stated outright.

verdicts.claim: The wal_checkpoint pragma returns three columns. The first is 1 when a RESTART, FULL or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked. The second is
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'single row with three integer columns. The first column is usually 0 but will be 1 if a RESTART or FULL or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked'; -1 values come from c3ref.

verdicts.claim: If automatic checkpointing is disabled and nothing else checkpoints, the WAL grows without limit. The SQLite docs also say that a larg
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'If an application disables the automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file from growing excessively'; read performance degrades as WAL grows; 'running checkpoints at regular intervals'.

verdicts.claim: Litestream runs three checkpoint tiers after each sync. A regular PASSIVE checkpoint runs at 1,000 pages (about 4 MB). A time-based PA
verdicts.evidence: Litestream guide: 'three complementary checkpoint mechanisms, evaluated in this order after each sync'; 'truncate-page-n: 121359 # Default : ~500MB'; 'checkpoint-interval: 1m'; 'Only runs if WAL has at least 1 page'.

verdicts.claim: Litestream takes over checkpointing. It starts a long-running read transaction so no other process can checkpoint or restart the WAL,
verdicts.evidence: how-it-works: 'Litestream works by effectively taking over the checkpointing process. It starts a long-running read transaction to prevent any other process from checkpointing and restarting the WAL file.'

verdicts.claim: A checkpoint cannot reset the WAL in the middle of a write transaction. A long write transaction, such as a large VACUUM, can therefor
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction'; PhotoStructure: 'The entire rebuilt database gets written to the WAL file'.

verdicts.claim: TRUNCATE checkpoints block writes until all read transactions finish. Long-lived readers therefore cause write outages.
verdicts.evidence: Litestream guide: 'TRUNCATE checkpoints will block writes until all read transactions complete. Long-lived readers cause extended write outages.'

verdicts.claim: If at least one reader is always active, no checkpoint completes and the WAL grows without bound. SQLite's WAL page lists three causes
verdicts.evidence: wal.html section 6 lists 'Disabling the automatic checkpoint mechanism', 'Checkpoint starvation', 'Very large write transactions'; 'the WAL file will grow without bound'.

verdicts.claim: A timer-based checkpointer under constant read load may never find a moment with no active reader, so it cannot truncate the WAL. Syn
verdicts.evidence: Syncthing post: 'As our application level checkpointer is timer based, we might never hit a timewindow without an active reader'; it names 'multiple gigabytes' as a critical level to act on, not a measured size. A related Syncthing thread found by search reports WALs of 33-45 GB.

verdicts.claim: A read transaction left open for hours blocks removal of every WAL page written after it started. A Syncthing team reported this in a
verdicts.evidence: Syncthing post: 'If a transaction is open for hours, we can't remove pages written to the WAL after its start.'
